global.headline: NVIDIA’S BOARD PREPARES TO REMOVE THE MAN WHO BUILT IT AFTER A SECOND AFFAIR SURFACES INSIDE THE COMPANY
summary: Nvidia’s board is preparing to oust chief executive Jensen Huang over two extramarital affairs and was due to meet as soon as Wednesday to decide his future, the Wall Street Journal reported. Hours earlier the New York Times reported, on five company employees, that the second relationship was with Kimberly Powell, Nvidia’s vice-president of healthcare, who reported directly to him. Nvidia did not respond to requests for comment. The shares bounced 3 per cent in the regular session on CoreWeave’s results, then fell about 8 per cent after hours; the US$4 trillion (S$5.12 trillion) chipmaker has shed more than US$300bn (S$384bn) since the first affair was reported.

The board’s outside inquiry, run by Wachtell, Lipton partner Joon Kim, is examining whether Huang was targeted by foreign intelligence through Alice Huang, the Megaspeed executive US intelligence says facilitated chip shipments to Chinese firms. CNN reported that Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent confronted Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick in the Situation Room last Thursday over his refusal to put Megaspeed on the entity list; Lutnick, briefed months ago on the affair, committed to nothing, and Commerce has added no company to that list in over a year. Megaspeed, a Singapore-incorporated firm renamed from the Chinese games developer 7Road International, has bought over US$4bn (S$5.12bn) of Nvidia chips by analyst estimates.
global.geopolitical: The chokepoint of the AI race now has a succession crisis inside it. Huang personally negotiated the terms on which American chips reach China; removing him hands that file to a board under congressional scrutiny and a Commerce Department no longer using its main export-control tool.
global.socioeconomic: An exit at a company this size is an index risk, not a governance footnote: pension and CPF-linked funds hold it passively. Megaspeed’s Singapore incorporation also puts the Republic’s AI-cloud role under American scrutiny, with analysts expecting tighter vetting of South-east Asian providers.

global.headline: WASHINGTON SETS ITSELF A TWO-WEEK CLOCK ON IRAN, ITS TREASURY SECRETARY MOVES ONTO A MILITARY BASE, AND CONGRESS DECLINES TO INTERVENE
summary: Mehdi Mohammadi, adviser to chief negotiator Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf, said on Telegram that the Americans had set a timeframe of about two weeks after which Trump would decide on military action, that Washington is preparing a limited strike and Iran a response, and that the US reply to Tehran’s Hormuz proposals was “not only unsatisfactory but completely deceptive” — no frozen funds released, no sanctions lifted, no halt in Lebanon. Iran refused Vice-President J.D. Vance’s request for a direct meeting. If sanctions hold, he wrote, a pre-emptive war would be needed “to increase the cost of sanctions for the enemy”.

Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, who has run the pressure campaign Operation Economic Outcast since August, has moved from his Washington home to a military base after Iranian threats to his life, joining Rubio and Stephen Miller; Iran reportedly geo-located his US$12.5m (S$16m) mansion from a published photograph. Security-council secretary Mohsen Rezaei told Moscow not “a particle” of Iran’s enriched uranium would leave, and warned that any base launching aircraft at Iran would be struck. At Arlington on Veterans Day Trump said the war — 23 US service members dead — would end “soon” and that Tehran started it; the House had voted 211-204 the previous evening to bury Thomas Massie’s impeachment articles against Pete Hegseth in committee, 11 Democrats absent, more than the margin.
global.geopolitical: The two tracks have swapped places: the strike threat Trump withdrew on Monday returns as a dated deadline, while the pressure instrument is a land blockade needing Iraq, Turkey, Pakistan and the Caspian states to cooperate — and the New York Times reports those neighbours resisting.
global.socioeconomic: Brent near US$93, with Saudi output close to its prewar 9.3m barrels a day, is why the blockade has not yet reached the world’s consumers — and why Tehran reads suffocation as the plan. Tuesday’s vote means no congressional constraint before 3 January.

global.headline: ABU DHABI ENDS WITH A PRISONER SWAP AND NOTHING ELSE, AND TRUMP’S ENVOYS FLY ON TO MOSCOW
summary: The second day of Russia-Ukraine talks in Abu Dhabi broke up in under two hours with no breakthrough. Jared Kushner announced that he and Steve Witkoff would fly to Moscow on Thursday to meet Putin, then to Dublin to see Zelenskyy, to work on “some openings and some opportunities”. Zelenskyy said the two days produced an “important humanitarian agreement” on a new prisoner exchange, plus security-guarantee talks. Vladimir Medinsky said understanding was reached in some areas and not others; Ukraine’s Davyd Arakhamia said Moscow came with “very strict directives”, one of the toughest rounds since 2022.

The unresolved question is who sits at the table. Kushner said he would press to bring European countries in, and Rubio, at the G7 in Paris, wants them “represented at that table directly”. Sergey Lavrov called their presence in the UAE not a “promising approach”, Dmitry Peskov said no Russian-EU contacts were planned or took place, and the Europeans met the Americans and Ukrainians separately. Zelenskyy insisted Europe “must be represented at all stages of substantive diplomacy”.
global.geopolitical: Two days of the first substantive negotiations since February produced one prisoner exchange, which is the measure of the distance on territory and guarantees. Taking the proposals to Putin directly keeps the bilateral channel Moscow prefers and leaves Europe in an adjoining room.
global.socioeconomic: A prisoner exchange is the one deliverable that changes lives at once and costs neither side a concession. For a war economy whose Kryvyi Rih and Zaporizhzhia steel plants are already shut by missile strikes, nothing in two days alters the winter ahead.

global.headline: FOUR MILLION SPANIARDS STOP WORK OVER THE PRICE OF A HOME
summary: Four million workers joined Spain’s first general strike since 2012 on Wednesday, called by the UGT and CCOO unions with tenants’ associations over housing costs; the tenants’ union expected five million of 23 million workers by day’s end. The unions reported 90 per cent stoppages at ports and in the car industry, with total halts at Volkswagen in Navarre and SEAT in Barcelona. Electricity demand fell 15.5 per cent between 10 and 11am and Madrid’s peak metro use was down 42 per cent on last week. Police reported 40 arrests from 476 incidents; the unions will file a complaint over a tear-gas operation that injured 20.

Spain is short about 750,000 homes, a gap the central bank expects to pass a million by 2028, and average rent of €1,176 (about S$1,683) equals 98.7 per cent of a young person’s average monthly salary, the Youth Council says. Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez, who called the 29 November snap election after decrees curbing evictions and rent rises were voted down, hopes housing anger displaces the corruption cases; his Socialists still trail. BBVA Research puts the strike’s cost at 0.1–0.2 per cent of annual GDP.
global.geopolitical: Housing is now the organising grievance of European politics, and the first country to strike over it does so eighteen days before a national election. Madrid’s answer will be read as a test case by governments facing the same shortfall.
global.socioeconomic: A rent consuming almost an entire youth salary is a labour-market constraint, not only a household one — Spain’s business lobby opposed the strike on exactly that ground. Ports and car plants stopped while services and finance largely worked, which shows where union power now sits.

global.headline: INDONESIA’S VICE-PRESIDENT RESIGNS OVER A SCHOOL CERTIFICATE, AND THE RULING ALLIANCE BEGINS TO COME APART
summary: Vice-President Gibran Rakabuming Raka resigned on Wednesday, his aide Budi Arie Setiadi told Reuters, having told President Prabowo Subianto of his intention the day before. The Supreme Court ruled the high-school certificate he used in the 2024 campaign invalid, after court rulings last month found his education documents did not meet election requirements; more than 100 legislators from across the parties petitioned on Wednesday for his impeachment. Senior law minister Yusril Ihza Mahendra said the upper house must convene to declare the vacancy and ask the president for two names. Prabowo did not mention it publicly and it is unclear whether he has accepted it.

Gibran is the son of former president Joko Widodo, and his place on the ticket was what carried Jokowi’s machine to Prabowo — made possible by a Constitutional Court ruling on the age requirement issued under Jokowi’s brother-in-law. Prabowo is already in a widening rift with his predecessor, in a country where anger over wildfire smoke and living costs has collapsed his approval.
global.geopolitical: South-east Asia’s largest economy enters a constitutional process with no settled successor, while the region negotiates haze enforcement and its own position between Washington and Beijing. If the Jokowi alliance breaks, Prabowo’s parliamentary supermajority loosens first.
global.socioeconomic: Jakarta’s uncertainty prices into the rupiah and regional risk premiums before it changes any policy, and Singapore is the exposed neighbour: Indonesia is among its largest trading partners and its counterparty on haze, the Riau power and carbon-capture deals and regional labour flows.

singapore.headline: A THIRD HEALTHCARE PROVIDER BREACHED IN A WEEK, AND A DEMENTIA APP SENDS NOTIFICATIONS NOBODY AUTHORISED
summary: Minmed Group said on Wednesday that a system supporting its teleconsultation and health-screening business was hit by a malicious cyberattack — the third healthcare provider breached here in a week, after Doctor Anywhere and Fullerton Health. Minmed, which runs clinics at Paragon, United Square, AMK Hub and JEM, said clinical records were untouched, engaged Ensign InfoSecurity, which validated its fixes on 5 November, and reported to the PDPC and the police. Fullerton Health disclosed that a server for its Migrant Worker Primary Care Plan — mandatory for work permit and S Pass holders in construction, marine and process work — was accessed without authorisation on 31 October, exposing names, FIN numbers, birth dates and contact details but no medical or financial data; it has not said how many workers are affected.

Dementia Singapore told CARA app users by e-mail on Wednesday that names, e-mail addresses, phone numbers and membership IDs may have been exposed on 1 November, and that it learned of the breach only when unauthorised notifications went out through its third-party app provider; no NRIC numbers were taken. SingHealth Polyclinics separately warned of fake messages sent in its name. The run now takes in insurers, Singapore Airlines, M1, SPH Media, SATS and these four, with the PDPC investigating.
singapore.geopolitical: Each was breached through a standalone system or an outsourced app — the pattern the Cyber Security Agency keeps warning about, where the perimeter that matters is the vendor’s. It lands a week after CSA awarded S$5.6m to tools policing what software agents can reach.
singapore.socioeconomic: The most exposed groups are the least able to respond: migrant workers on an employer-bought plan, and dementia patients and carers phished through the app built to support them. Teaching those households to distrust health notifications costs appointments no PDPC penalty recovers.

singapore.headline: HDB’S DEFICIT NARROWS TO S$4.7 BILLION AS APPLICATIONS FOR NEW FLATS HIT A FOUR-YEAR HIGH
summary: The Housing Board recorded a net deficit of S$4.7bn in the financial year to March 2026, down from S$6.34bn, its annual report shows: a S$5.13bn core shortfall offset by a S$419m surplus from commercial property. Home ownership was S$4bn of it — S$1.75bn on flat sales, S$1.31bn in expected losses on flats being built, S$711m in CPF grants to resale and EC buyers. Upgrading deficits fell to S$279m as Home Improvement Programme works wound down. HDB completed 15,417 flats against 20,294 a year earlier, had 100,122 under construction and handed keys to 19,254 households. The grant funding the gap was S$4.73bn, taking grants since 1960 to S$66.23bn.

Demand rose with the income ceilings. By 5pm on Wednesday the November exercise had drawn 35,603 applicants for 7,964 flats — 4.5 per flat, the highest rate since August 2022 and the most applications since October 2024, against 22,600 in June. National Development Minister Chee Hong Tat said the rise was expected given the new S$16,000 family and S$8,000 singles ceilings; the median first-timer family rate rose from 1.4 to 2.6. Four-room flats at Toa Payoh Hillside, a Prime project with an 11 per cent clawback and a top price of S$832,000, drew over six applicants each; Tengah’s two-room flexi units were 18 times oversubscribed among singles.
singapore.geopolitical: A housing programme funded by a disclosed annual Budget transfer is Singapore’s answer to the argument being made on the streets of Madrid — and the reason the same shortage yields a general strike there and an oversubscribed ballot here.
singapore.socioeconomic: The deficit narrowed because fewer flats were completed, not because they cost less to build, so the bill returns as the 100,122 units under construction are handed over. Raising the ceilings widened the queue faster than supply: 4.5 applicants a flat means most newly eligible buyers wait again.

singapore.headline: MOH PROPOSES LETTING TEENAGERS GET MENTAL HEALTH CARE WITHOUT A PARENT’S CONSENT
summary: The Health Ministry opened a public consultation on Wednesday, running to 8 December, on guidelines that treat parental consent as a barrier to young people getting mental health care. Consent would be tiered by service: required below 13 for screening and assessments that do not produce a diagnosis, and sought for psychotherapeutic services including school counselling and cognitive behavioural therapy. Where it cannot be obtained, a professional could still treat a young person of at least 13 judged mature enough to decide, if that is in their best interest. If a teenager refuses to have parents approached, or parents refuse, professionals are told to explore the reasons rather than stop.

The ministry cited the Singapore Youth Epidemiology and Resilience Study finding that about one in three people aged 10 to 18 report symptoms of depression, anxiety or other conditions, and a 2022 Institute of Mental Health study that 70 per cent of those sought no professional help. A third of such conditions begin before 14, MOH said, warning that failure to identify them raises the risk of poor educational attainment, unemployment, chronic illness and substance misuse.
singapore.geopolitical: Singapore is proposing in guidance what other jurisdictions legislate as a mature-minor doctrine. Set at 13, the threshold would be among the region’s lower ones, and it arrives the same month as MDDI’s finding that parents prefer tiered social-media access to a ban.
singapore.socioeconomic: A 70 per cent non-help-seeking rate against a one-in-three symptom rate is the gap the guidelines address, and school counselling is where that volume appears first. The constraint is supply: consent at 13 only shortens the wait if a counsellor is there at the end of it.

word.definition: A final settling or discharge; something that puts an end to a matter or quietly kills it off.
word.etymology: From the mediaeval Latin quietus est, “he is quit” — the formula written on a receipt to show a debt discharged and an account closed. Shakespeare gave it its English afterlife in Hamlet’s “make his quietus”, and it has carried the sense of a quiet, procedural ending ever since.
word.example: The House gave Massie’s impeachment articles their quietus by 211 votes to 204, not by acquitting Hegseth but by referring him to a committee that will never report.
